title: Moody's Warns AI Spending Threatens Big Tech Credit as Google's Cash Flow Turns Negative
excerpt: Hyperscaler capital expenditure is set to reach $785 billion this year and close in on $1 trillion by 2027, as Google reports the first negative free cash flow in its history as a public company.
body:
• Google reported negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in Q2 2026, the first time the company has burned cash since going public.
  • Moody's Ratings now projects hyperscaler capex at $785 billion for 2026, up from $700 billion forecast in March, closing in on $1 trillion by 2027.
  • The ratings agency flagged $662 billion in off-balance-sheet data center lease obligations among top tech firms as a growing credit risk.
  • Apple, which has largely avoided the AI spending race, has outperformed its hyperscaler peers in the stock market this year.

Google's Historic Cash Burn

Google's parent company Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in the second quarter of 2026, a figure that would have been unthinkable for a company long defined by its cash-generating machine. It is the first time Alphabet has burned cash since becoming a publicly traded company in 2004.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OFZMlqaXACM

The culprit is capital expenditure on AI infrastructure. Alphabet raised its spending guidance to $205 billion for the full year, up from $180 billion to $190 billion forecast earlier, and warned that capital expenditures will "increase significantly in 2027." Analysts expect that number to reach at least $262 billion next year.

"We expect that free cash flow will remain under pressure driven by our investments in technical infrastructure, which enable us to capitalize on the AI opportunity."

— Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet CFO

Moody's Sounds the Alarm

Moody's Ratings revised its hyperscaler capex forecast sharply upward this week, projecting $785 billion in combined spending for 2026 across Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet, Oracle and CoreWeave. That figure is $85 billion higher than the agency's March projection and puts the industry on track to approach $1 trillion in annual capital expenditure by 2027.

The agency identified a growing structural risk: $662 billion in off-balance-sheet data center lease obligations spread across major tech firms. These implicit debts do not appear on traditional balance sheets but could pressure credit metrics sharply if the anticipated returns on AI investment fail to materialize within the next two years.

The spending is backed by surging demand. Combined revenue growth from AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud hit its fastest pace since Q2 2021. AI revenue run rates have climbed to $15 billion at AWS and $37 billion at Microsoft, the latter growing 123 percent year-on-year. Moody's noted that AI providers OpenAI and Anthropic are themselves struggling to find computing capacity to meet demand.

The Trillion-Dollar Bet

What sets this cycle apart from previous tech investment booms is the speed and scale of debt accumulation. J.P. Morgan analysts have estimated that the high-grade bond market may need to absorb $1.5 trillion in AI data center bond sales over the next five years, potentially representing more than 20 percent of the entire investment-grade bond market by 2030.

Moody's Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi has drawn parallels to the dot-com era but noted a critical difference: internet companies in the late 1990s were funded primarily by stocks and venture capital. The AI buildout is being financed with corporate debt at a pace that exceeds anything in the dot-com period, even after adjusting for inflation.

Winners and Losers in the AI Arms Race

The divergence between AI spenders and AI abstainers is becoming stark. Apple, which has largely steered clear of the infrastructure arms race, has outperformed its hyperscaler peers in the stock market this year and briefly dethroned Nvidia as the most valuable company last week. The contrast underscores growing investor anxiety about whether the returns will justify the spending.

Google's earnings call offered a mixed picture. Cloud revenue hit $24.77 billion for the quarter, up 82 percent from a year ago. But search revenue, the company's core profit engine, fell below analyst expectations despite CEO Sundar Pichai saying search usage hit an all-time high during the World Cup. Meanwhile, the company's latest AI model, Gemini 3.6 Flash, appears to trail recent releases from OpenAI and Anthropic in major benchmarks.

The Indian Tech Connection

For the Indian technology sector, the AI spending cycle carries both opportunity and risk. Indian IT services companies are major beneficiaries of cloud migration and AI implementation projects. But the underlying financial stress on their biggest clients raises questions about whether spending can be sustained if returns disappoint. Indian professionals in Silicon Valley also face ripple effects: any pullback in AI investment could trigger the kind of hiring freezes and layoffs that followed previous tech corrections.
